synopsis: A program starting in October 2026 can realistically reach software-in-the-loop simulation with partly validated sensor models by mid-2027, but credibility belongs to the model, configuration, intended use and evidence—not to a platform intrinsically [f65, f7755]. Sensor and environment fidelity remain the hardest uncertainty: no accepted qualification method was found for off-road dust, snow or fog, no off-road fidelity thresholds were found, and degraded-visibility conditions are least validated [f10424, f331, f5220, f7886]. Clear-weather sensor accuracy can be high when the complete signal chain is modeled: one ray-traced lidar study reported errors of 1.7% for amplitude, 8.5% for point count and 9.3% for mean intensity, but field dust behavior is not captured by simple attenuation models [f4416, f4417, f4426]. No validated off-road operator model was found; on-road warning-benefit estimates ranged from 53% to 96% depending on the driver model, illustrating the importance of behavioral assumptions [f250, f3040, f3045]. Greater vehicle-model complexity does not imply greater accuracy, yet articulated maneuvers and hydrostatic braking require appropriate physical detail rather than universally simplified representations [f5908, f6028, f6049, f6050]. Planning should identify the physical measurements validating each model, experimentally correlate adverse-environment sensors, and retain physical testing where models are weak; rare-event methods cannot establish claims about sensor physics outside simulation scope [f10229, f5219, f10470, f6853].
